newsitem.title: USA: Dollar falls after tame inflation data fuels rate hike doubts.
newsitem.headline: Dollar falls after tame inflation data fuels rate hike doubts.

text.p: NEW YORK, March 14 - The dollar fell against the German mark and was barely changed versus the Japanese yen on Friday after a surprisingly tame inflation report prompted doubts that the Federal Reserve will soon raise interest rates and traders took profits ahead of the weekend.

A Labour Department report showed the producer price index, a key barometer of inflationary pressures, declined in February by a greater amount than most Wall Street economists had expected. Furthermore, the core index, which excludes volatile food and energy items, unexpectedly edged lower.

Market participants seemed to pay more attention to the inflation news rather than a Fed report on industrial production and capacity utilization that showed the manufacturing sector remains in good shape.

Fed policy makers meet on March 25 to decide whether they need to tighten credit to keep price pressures in check. The benign inflation data released on Friday seemed to indicate a rate hike may not be necessary.

Higher rates typically help the dollar by making deposits denominated in that currency more attractive to foreign investors. Fading hopes for a rate increase, however, weighed on the dollar on Friday.

"This is predicated on the fact that the market has decided to concentrate on the inflation factor of today's news and has disregarded what can be extrapolated as positive strong signs coming out of the capacity utilization numbers and the industrial production," said Hillel Waxman, a first vice president of Bank Leumi Trust Co of New York.
"But who ever is trading dollars has pretty much said they're going with the mentality that there is no hike," Waxman said.
The dollar traded as high as 1.71 marks and 124.11 yen on Friday. Traders said the mark's sharp gains against the Japanese currency also helped the dollar to rise versus the yen.
Purchases of marks for yen are oftened funnelled through the dollar.
In late trade on Friday, the dollar fetched 1.6952 marks, down from 1.7047 marks on Thursday. The dollar cost 123.45 yen, up slightly from 123.34 yen.
The dollar fell to 1.4555 Swiss francs from 1.4650 francs. The British pound rose to $1.6007 from $1.5973. The dollar was unchanged at Canadian $1.3650.

The dollar had climbed above 124 yen early in the day on a news report quoting prominent economist Rudiger Dornbusch as saying Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin would act to curb the dollar if it climbed past 130 yen. Yet the dollar erased the bulk of these gains later in the session.

"That caught peoples eye, but I mean, it was very quickly dispelled by the market," said Ben Strauss, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Bank Julius Baer and Co. in New York. "If Rubin has something to say, we are going to hear it from Rubin."

Profit-taking also pressured the dollar as the week drew to a close. Some traders also noted that some market participants were disappointed when the dollar failed to climb above 1.71 marks on Friday.
